subject: Question on noise term in the Gaussian Process code in the manual

messages.author: e1c430550f86b1f6
messages.subject: Question on noise term in the Gaussian Process code in the manual
parts:
Hi all,

I'm very new to GP and had some difficulties in following this from the manual:

In ref manual v2.6.2, Ch 14.4 Predictive Inference with a Gaussian Process -> Analytical Form of Joint Predictive Inference (pg 144):

In the same code regarding omega (copied from Github):
for (i in 1:N2)
   for (j in 1:N2)
     Omega[i,j] <- exp(-pow(x2[i] - x2[j],2))
      + if_else(i==j, 0.1, 0.0);


Questions:
1. What is the motivation for adding the ifelse(....) term here?
- Ch2 of RW (GP for machine learning) seems to suggest that the noise term is needed for K(X,X) (which I assume translate to Sigma as per Stan manual) only to take care of noisy observations.
- Similar in Andrew's book (pg. 503, 3rd edition), sigma^2 is "added" to K(x,x) only.

2. It seems that the sample code is built for fixed covar function. But, I'm looking at a situation where I first have to fit the GP with training data and then do prediction with test data. In this case, would I still need to add the noise term to omega (which is done in the generated quantities block)?

Many thanks,
Andy

Exactly --- sometimes called "jitter" in this context.

>

In this case, would I still need to add the noise term to omega (which is done in the generated quantities block)?

I'm pretty sure you do if you want to strictly simulate from the process.
If you just want mean predictions, you don't need any noise at all.

In that way, I think it's like usual regression in that (x[n] * beta) gives
you the expectation and then epsilon[n] adds noise.

- Bob

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on noise term in the Gaussian Process code in the manual
parts:
We had some discussion off-list (insights below are due to Aki) and here's a summary for posterity...

1. The manual doesn't match GPML or BDA, so we're going to fix that. Here's what it'll say:

Omega[i,j] <- exp(-pow(x2[i] - x2[j],2));

Note that if you wanted the posterior distribution over y, rather than the latent function f, you would want to do it the way it's done currently in the manual, with an extra variance 0.1 on the main diagonal. But usually you're interested in posterior inference about f, so there's no need for that extra term.

2. Question: Why are length-scales sometimes parameterized as rho^2 and sometimes as l^2, where rho^2 =1/l^2? 
Answer: Choosing l^2 is better for interpretation's sake because then it's in the same units as x (well, l is in the same units...) Both should be constrained to be positive (lower=0), and in terms of sampling both are log-transformed with log(rho^2)=-log(l^2), so they should be equivalent with respect to sampling efficiency.

Seth

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on noise term in the Gaussian Process code in the manual
parts:
1. The manual doesn't match GPML or BDA, so we're going to fix that. Here's what it'll say:

for (i in 1:N2)
    for (j in 1:N2)
      Omega[i,j] <- exp(-pow(x2[i] - x2[j],2));

Note that if you wanted the posterior distribution over y, rather than the latent function f, you would want to do it the way it's done currently in the manual, with an extra variance 0.1 on the main diagonal. But usually you're interested in posterior inference about f, so there's no need for that extra term.

Careful — the GP prior is often assumed to not have a diagonal component but
there’s no reason why it can’t.  Even when using the GP to model some prior
directly it can be useful to add a diagonal term.

2. Question: Why are length-scales sometimes parameterized as rho^2 and sometimes as l^2, where rho^2 =1/l^2? 
Answer: Choosing l^2 is better for interpretation's sake because then it's in the same units as x (well, l is in the same units...) Both should be constrained to be positive (lower=0), and in terms of sampling both are log-transformed with log(rho^2)=-log(l^2), so they should be equivalent with respect to sampling efficiency.

Again, this can be a subtle issue.  In particular, when we start using nontrivial
priors the two parameterizations will yield different posteriors*.  In other words, 
the sampling performance can be different because the priors can will be
different.  When thinking about length scales the l parameterization is more
interpretable and hence leads to better prior specification, and when thinking
about ARD the rho parameterization is more interpretable and head leads
to better prior specifications.

* Fun fact: cauchy(x) = cauchy(1/x) so the Half-Cauchy priors would actually
yield the same posterior in either case.

Seth
